title: The Judges Who Walk Between Gardens
summary: A physician’s civic reforms and traveling musicians support self-governing settlements divided by occupation and competing charters.
history: Suth’s garden communes elected judges rather than inheriting a sovereign. In 943 a physician reformer sought to reduce the separate courts maintained by armed households and funerary custodians. His ally withdrew support when those institutions threatened revolt. Traveling musicians carried arguments between valleys, blending older measures with instruments learned in exile. An outside authority later occupied the eastern gardens while the western communes retained a different charter. When a public vote ended occupation, departing forces destroyed channels and records. Returning households therefore faced reconstruction before constitutional celebration. The elected judges now walk between settlements to hear claims, because neither the old exemptions nor the new vote can make water flow through a broken canal.
question: how elected courts can rebuild channels while deciding which occupation-era transactions were coerced and which present households depend upon them.
transformations: A physician-reformer confronting military and religious privileges becomes an attempt to unite practical civic jurisdiction.
Exiled musicians blending traditions and carrying political memory become a traveling valley ensemble using pre-industrial instruments.
Partition, occupation, a independence vote, and destructive withdrawal become the eastern gardens’ interrupted self-government.
Rural communal autonomy and elected adjudicators become walking judges without a hereditary sovereign.
rows: Valen the Basin Physician

Valen treated soldiers and gardeners through the same queue, then proposed ending their separate courts. His former ally called the reform dangerous. Surviving patient accounts show ordinary cooperation persisting after the political alliance collapsed.
The Eastern Broken Gardens

Returning households found gates burned and channels blocked. Constitutional visitors planted ceremonial trees before supplying tools. Gardeners recorded both gifts, demonstrating that symbolic return and practical recovery were different achievements.
The Walking Judges

Judges visit gardens rather than requiring every claimant to travel. Their elections exclude servants in several communes. Reformers propose widening the electorate while preserving the accessible hearings that already provide a genuine alternative to inherited office.
The Ally’s Reversal

Valen’s ally withdrew support after privileged courts threatened supply boycotts. Later songs describe personal treachery alone. Grain accounts reveal the threat’s force, explaining the choice without removing responsibility for abandoning promised reforms.
The Exile’s Reed Lute

The lute combines a local body with a tuning learned abroad. Cultural custodians call the arrangement impure. Musicians show how changed materials allowed continuity in exile, refusing an account of heritage that would prohibit the adaptations sustaining it.
The Judge’s Shared Meal

Claimants eat together before a hearing if they consent. Refusal does not count against a case. The limit prevents hospitality from becoming forced reconciliation, particularly where people harmed during occupation face neighbors who benefited from their absence.
The Charter of No Inherited Seat

The charter forbids hereditary judges but leaves eligibility tied to landholding. Families maintain influence through property. Readers distinguish the real achievement of elected office from the claim that election alone eliminated inherited power.
The Channel Root Eel

Small eels travel through root-lined irrigation channels and disappear when gates remain closed too long. Gardeners use their return to assess reconnection. Celebrants call them liberated ancestors, overlooking the living habitat that reconstruction has restored.
The Judges’ Graft Road

The road follows settlements needing seasonal graft inspections, allowing hearings and practical instruction on one journey. Wealthier communes seek priority visits. Judges publish travel costs and unmet requests so exclusion cannot disappear behind their title of universal service.
The Coerced Transfer Review

Occupation-era deeds require inquiry into actual consent and subsequent dependency. The rule does not void every transfer automatically. It creates space for restitution that recognizes both original harm and households now relying on a garden they acquired under different circumstances.
Iren of the Exiled Measures

Iren carried songs between valleys while recovering from an injured hand. Younger musicians adapted her parts rather than replacing her. Their ensemble’s continuity depended on accommodation, contradicting patrons’ image of rebellion as effortless youthful vigor.
The West Charter Orchard

This orchard remained beyond occupation but sold food to occupying troops. Residents claim untouched independence. Accounts reveal dependence and compromise, allowing acknowledgment without equating their choices with every act of the occupation authority.
The Returning Tool Pools

Households pool tools before debating final ownership. The arrangement preserves urgent planting while claims remain open. Wealthy donors demand votes proportional to tools lent, threatening to convert reconstruction assistance into authority over the courts reviewing old coercion.
The Vote and the Gate Fires

The vote ended outside rule but departing forces burned gatehouses and channel controls. Later ceremonies merge decision and liberation into one moment. Reconstruction records show years of labor required before many households experienced the freedom publicly announced.
The Physician’s Two Queue Tiles

One tile once marked soldiers and the other gardeners. Valen turned both downward beneath a shared bench. Curators want them displayed upright, while patients prefer the bench’s continued use as evidence that the institutional distinction was practically challenged.
The Song’s Visiting Verse

Each host garden adds a verse naming its current repair need. Distant audiences prefer a fixed performance. Musicians retain the changing verse, keeping the ensemble connected to practical communities rather than becoming a portable image of rebellion.
The First Return Inventories

Inventories distinguish destruction, neglect, and supplies taken by neighbors. Their precision prevents every loss being assigned to one dramatic withdrawal. It also names local beneficiaries whose role later patriotic accounts preferred to omit.
The Judge’s Empty Footsteps

Footsteps recur on an abandoned hearing path after a claimant dies unanswered. Rain channels explain some sounds but not their timing. Judges have begun recording postponed cases publicly, responding to an actual unfinished duty without claiming certainty about the phenomenon.
Graft Recovery Teaching

Teachers demonstrate grafts using local rootstocks and bounded water. Reconstruction donors supply prestigious imported varieties poorly suited to damaged channels. Gardeners request useful materials instead, turning gratitude into a negotiation over what assistance can actually accomplish.
The Servants’ Election Petition

Servants maintain communal channels but cannot elect the judges ruling upon their work. Their petition invokes contribution rather than a fictitious ancient charter. Commune leaders must decide whether self-government includes those whose labor makes the governing households viable.
